Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette:
Mark was thirty-three, a graphic designer who had been divorced for just over a year, when he finally walked into a therapist’s office. He did not want to be there. What drove him was a growing dread that he was losing control of a life he had already seen shatter once. The trouble had started on a humid September night three years earlier. He had been at a crowded downtown bar with friends, the kind of place he used to love for its noise and energy. Around midnight, police swarmed the building—noise complaint that escalated, someone had flashed a weapon, and within seconds the room became a chaos of shouting and flashlights. Mark was shoved to the sticky floor, his face pressed against the tiles, a boot on his back and the cold ring of a gun muzzle against his skull. He had done nothing wrong, but for what felt like an eternity he was certain he would die there, face-down, unable to move or breathe.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to narrow. The first trigger he noticed was the dark. Leaving his graphic design studio after sunset—which in autumn came early—sent a bolt of alertness through his chest that made his hands shake over the keyboard. He started leaving before dusk, missing deadlines, claiming he had appointments. Then came the cars: the specific model of the police cruiser that had screamed to a stop outside the bar. Whenever he spotted one—a black-and-white sedan with that particular grille—his stomach dropped and he would pull over, heart hammering, until it passed. Crowds became unbearable. The press of bodies in a subway car or a grocery aisle reminded him of the bar that night, of not being able to see an exit, of being pinned down. Each trigger fed the next, and Mark learned that the fastest way to loosen the knot in his chest was to drink. A beer at lunch became three by early afternoon. He discovered that a few shots of whiskey before driving home made the dark roads tolerable. He started keeping a flask in his desk drawer.

The causal chain tightened over months. Nighttime drove him to drink; similar cars drove him to drink; crowded places drove him to drink. And when alcohol was not enough or was unavailable, he developed other tactics. He began covering his face with his hands whenever a police cruiser passed—a reflexive gesture, as if he could make himself invisible. He avoided any street where he might encounter a uniformed officer or a marked vehicle. He stopped visiting the part of town where the bar was located, rerouted his commute by miles, and turned down freelance projects that required him to attend events or work late. His wife could not understand why he would not go out with her, why he was drinking secretly, why he flinched when she touched him from behind. She left after a year of trying. Mark did not fight it; he was too exhausted.

By the time he sat in the intake chair, his life was small. He worked from home as much as possible, but his boss had started to notice missed deadlines and refused requests to meet clients. The drinking had crept into mornings. What finally brought him in was not insight but panic: last week, leaving a late meeting in the dark, he saw a sedan that matched the police car’s silhouette, and before he knew it he was crouched on the sidewalk, hands over his face, shaking uncontrollably. A stranger asked if he needed help. He could not answer. Now he was here, hoping for a way out of the loop, terrified that nothing would work.
